title: People think the story of Lazarus is only about resurrection.
paragraphs: People think the story of Lazarus is only about resurrection.
But if you slow down long enough to listen carefully to the tension inside John chapter 11… you realize something terrifying and beautiful is happening beneath the surface.
Jesus was not late.
He was deliberate.
And the “four days” were not random.
They were a divine collision between Jewish burial tradition, prophetic symbolism, messianic revelation, spiritual corruption, and God’s power over what humanity had already declared impossible.
Most believers know Jesus raised Lazarus.
Very few understand why He waited four days.
That detail changes everything.
In John 11:6, Scripture says:
“When therefore he heard that he was sick, he abode two days still in the same place where he was.”
The Greek wording is shocking.

The phrase:
“ἔμεινεν οὖν δύο ἡμέρας”
(emeinen oun duo hēmeras)

Literally means:
“He remained… therefore… two days.”
Jesus intentionally stayed.
Not accidentally delayed.
Not distracted.
Not overwhelmed.
He stayed on purpose while someone He loved was dying.
That alone breaks modern shallow theology.
Because sometimes Jesus loves you deeply… and still allows the situation to reach the funeral stage.
The text says in John 11:5:
“Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus.”

The Greek word for loved is:
“ἠγάπα”
(ēgapa)
From agapaō — covenantal love, sacrificial love, divine committed love.
And immediately after telling us Jesus loved them…
the next verse says He stayed away.
That means His delay was connected to His love.
Not opposed to it.
Somebody reading this has been interpreting God’s silence as abandonment.
But heaven may be preparing resurrection through delay.
Then comes the most overlooked detail in the entire narrative.
John 11:17:
“Then when Jesus came, he found that he had lain in the grave four days already.”
Four days.
Why does John specify that?
Because in first-century Jewish understanding, there was a common belief that the spirit hovered near the body for three days hoping to return.
After the fourth day, decomposition fully set in.
Hope was officially dead.
The Jerusalem Talmud hints at this cultural belief:
“For three days the soul hovers over the body intending to re-enter it, but when it sees that the appearance of the face has changed, it departs.”
This matters deeply.
Jesus intentionally arrived after every human explanation expired.
He waited until resurrection could not be misunderstood as resuscitation.
This was not revival.
This was absolute dominion over irreversible death.
And Martha confirms the horror of the moment.
John 11:39:
“Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days.”

The Greek phrase:
“ὄζει”
(ozei)

Means:
“He already smells.”
Decay had already testified against hope.
The body was decomposing.
Funeral grief had matured.
The mourners had accepted finality.
And Jesus walked directly into that impossibility.
Because Jesus specializes in entering situations after humans bury them emotionally.
But the mystery gets even deeper.

The name “Lazarus” comes from the Hebrew:
“אֶלְעָזָר”
(Elʿāzār)

Meaning:
“God has helped.”
Imagine the irony.
“God has helped” is lying dead in a tomb.
Some of you feel exactly like that right now.
The promises over your life feel buried.
Your prayer life feels buried.
Your purity feels buried.
Your marriage feels buried.
Your purpose feels buried.
Your joy feels buried.
And heaven seems four days late.
But Jesus often waits until human strength collapses so divine glory becomes undeniable.
Jesus Himself explains the deeper purpose in John 11:4:
“This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God might be glorified thereby.”

The Greek word for glory:
“δόξα”
(doxa)

Means:
manifested splendor,
revealed divine weight,
visible majesty.
Lazarus was not merely sick.
He was becoming a stage for revelation.
And then Jesus says something explosive in John 11:25:
“I am the resurrection, and the life.”

Greek:
“ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή”
(egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē)
“Egō eimi” was not casual speech.
It echoes the divine covenant name revealed to Moses in Exodus 3:14.

Hebrew:
“אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה”
(Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh)
“I AM THAT I AM.”
Jesus was not merely claiming power to resurrect.
He was identifying Himself as Resurrection itself.
Death was standing face to face with its Creator.
And death was about to lose.
Then comes the command.
John 11:43:
“Lazarus, come forth.”

Greek:
“Λάζαρε, δεῦρο ἔξω”
(Lazare, deuro exō)
“Come outside.”
Ancient preachers often noted something fascinating here:
Jesus called Lazarus by name because if He had only shouted “Come forth,” every grave might have emptied.
Because creation recognizes the voice of its King.
And Lazarus emerges.
Still wrapped.
Still bound.
Still carrying grave clothes.
Resurrected… but needing freedom.
John 11:44:
“Loose him, and let him go.”

Greek:
“λύσατε αὐτὸν καὶ ἄφετε ὑπάγειν”
(lysate auton kai aphete hypagein)
This is where many Christians stop too early.

Jesus can resurrect you instantly…
while sanctification still takes process.
Some people are alive spiritually but still wrapped in old mentalities, addictions, shame, fear, trauma, lust, pride, compromise, church hurt, and hidden sin.

Alive…
but bound.

Breathing…
but restricted.

Raised…
but tangled in grave clothes.

And Jesus still commands the community:
“Loose him.”
This story was never only about Lazarus.
It was about revealing Christ’s authority over the final enemy.
In Jewish thought, four days represented the point beyond recovery.
But Jesus intentionally chose the impossible timeline.
Because God gains the most glory from situations humans declare permanently dead.
And prophetically, Lazarus becomes a shadow of something greater.
Because not long after this miracle…
Jesus Himself would enter a tomb.
But unlike Lazarus, Jesus would not need someone else to call Him out.
He said in John 10:18:
“I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again.”
The resurrection of Lazarus pointed toward the greater resurrection still coming.
The empty tomb of Christ.
And that changes everything for every believer.
Because the Gospel is not self-improvement.
It is resurrection.
Not behavior modification.
Resurrection.
Not religious cosmetics.
Resurrection.
Dead hearts brought back to life through Jesus Christ.
Somebody reading this feels spiritually four days dead.
Dreams decomposing.
Faith decaying.
Hope suffocating.
But Jesus has never been intimidated by the smell of impossible situations.
He walks toward tombs.
He speaks into graves.
He calls dead things by name.
And what He calls… must answer.
Even the tomb had to surrender when the Voice of Life arrived.
